title: Dolby Makes No TVs or Phones: How Is 93% From Licensing?｜Curio Archive
description:
You see "Dolby" on TVs and phones, yet the company makes neither, and 93% of its revenue is licensing. How?
For anyone curious where that name comes from, or how a licensing business really works.

This episode starts in 1949 with a 16-year-old high school student working part-time at a tape recorder company. From there: a letter mailed to a patent lawyer from Afghanistan in 1965 on the drive back to England, a small company in a corner of a London clothing factory, one decision about the home version in 1967, a reel-to-reel deck that never made it into ordinary homes, the looked-down-on cassette, an order from the US FCC on Christmas Eve 1996, and finally how the latest annual report says Dolby charges. Along the way we check two popular claims against the record: "Dolby builds no hardware and only sells patents" and "Dolby's first film was A Clockwork Orange."

Easy to mishear: 93% is licensing's share of total revenue (rounded in the annual report), not a cut of each device, and the report does not say how much Dolby earns per unit. The Christmas Eve order covers only US terrestrial digital TV, not the whole world and not phones. TVs and set-top boxes are 34% of licensing revenue, which does not mean every TV has Dolby. Why the founder chose as he did, none of the records we read say. All figures are for fiscal 2025 (ended September 26, 2025); fiscal 2026 results are scheduled for November 17, 2026.

This channel has no partnership with the companies mentioned and takes no money from them. Sources are listed below.

Data as of 2026-10-31

t001.text: Ever seen the word “Dolby” on your TV or phone?

t002.text: If so, its maker usually pays Dolby a fee for every unit sold.

t004.text: So you may hear: Dolby makes no hardware, only sells patents.

t005.text: Yet its very first business sold machines it built itself.

t006.text: 1996: TV sound rule; a rival objects.

t007.text: Decades of fees on, its annual report still says it must keep persuading.

t008.text: Today I'm opening the file: how does a company that makes no TVs or phones get makers to pay it for every unit?

t009.text: To answer that, the story goes back to California in 1949, to a 16-year-old student.

t010.text: By chance, he got a weekend and holiday job at a tape recorder company.

t011.text: Tape had a flaw it couldn't shake: hiss. From then on, he wanted to beat it.

t012.text: If you've heard old tapes, you know that hissing noise.

t013.text: He later led electronics on the world's first practical VTR.

t014.text: I thought he'd make VTRs for life. But no.

t015.text: He went to Cambridge for a physics PhD.

t016.text: In 1963 he went to India, as a technical adviser on a UNESCO project.

t017.text: His hobby: recording local live music on tape.

t018.text: The hiss he'd fought since that job: how to kill it?

t019.text: Existing gear, he found, added more distortion than the noise it removed.

t020.text: What he realized: hiss is only audible when the music is quiet.

t021.text: At a lively party you can't hear the fridge hum; once the guests leave, it's back.

t022.text: So loud parts pass; only quiet parts get treated.

t023.text: In 1965, heading back to England, he drove overland for two months.

t024.text: On the way, in Afghanistan, he mailed the idea to a California patent lawyer.

t025.text: What would a letter mailed mid-trip become?

t026.text: That May, he set up in London.

t027.text: In a 1988 interview, he said it was a corner of a clothing factory.

t028.text: $25,000, saved and borrowed, plus four employees.

t029.text: Guess what he made first? The archive says: not sound, but noise reduction for black-and-white video.

t030.text: He showed the BBC; they passed, since the BBC was switching to color. How's that for timing?

t031.text: Back to sound: that trick went in a metal box by the recorder.

t032.text: This is A-type noise reduction: not a recorder, a hiss remover.

t033.text: Remember that first business? They built these boxes themselves.

t034.text: Buyers: studios in Britain and the US. And the first customer?

t035.text: Decca Records. Months of tests, then the first nine and three months' exclusivity.

t036.text: See? “No hardware” fails from the very first deal.

t037.text: Its first name, oddly, was “signal-to-noise stretcher,”

t038.text: soon it was just “Dolby,” which surprised even him.

t039.text: Remember this: a man's surname became a machine's name. Later, that name earns too.

t040.text: That's where Dolby started: a small firm building machines for studios.

t041.text: Then in 1967, an American audio maker asked for something entirely different.

t042.text: That was Henry Kloss, pushing for home noise reduction.

t043.text: That became B-type. The catch: who builds the home machines?

t044.text: Boxes sell. Home version: what would you do?

t045.text: Me? A bigger factory, and build it myself.

t047.text: They sold the design to existing audio makers, and built only pro machines themselves.

t048.text: The “only sells patents” story starts to fit only here, barely.

t049.text: Why they chose this, no record I read says.

t050.text: The question: could the first licensee deliver?

t052.text: It worked well, but tape on two big reels was a hassle; homes never really took to it.

t053.text: Awkward: no home units, and its first bet was on the wrong format.

t056.text: Per engineering history, cassettes ranked below reels and 8-tracks.

t058.text: But with Dolby, cassette sound could match vinyl.

t059.text: In 1970, the first cassette decks with B-type hit stores and took off.

t061.text: Dolby's chronology: just five that September, 30 by the end of the next year.

t062.text: Odder: the Afghanistan letter? The archive says it became a US patent,

t064.text: Decks shipped before it was granted, though earlier filings existed.

t065.text: So I think makers bought more than that one patent. What else?

t066.text: Designs, plus a name already in use. Remember that surname?

t067.text: An engineers' journal wrote: almost every deck maker licensed it.

t068.text: Had a cassette deck? Recall what its panel said.

t069.text: Only now did licensing work: let others build the home units.

t070.text: To get the name heard wider, it had to enter a pitch-dark place.

t071.text: The cinema. You may have heard: Dolby's first film was Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange.

t072.text: 1971. You might think the whole world heard Dolby then.

t073.text: But only for mixing and mastering the film.

t074.text: Theater prints still used plain optical sound.

t075.text: The name Dolby Stereo didn't exist yet.

t076.text: You may ask: which film first bore that name?

t078.text: Big theaters with speakers already went first. Why would small ones pay?

t079.text: The answer isn't Kubrick. It's Star Wars, in 1977.

t080.text: Its success first got small theaters into stereo.

t081.text: Switching meant a Dolby unit plus new speakers.

t082.text: Back on the machine-selling side. Noticed?

t083.text: Within ten years, 6,000 cinemas worldwide had Dolby Stereo.

t084.text: In 1992 it made surround digital: five main channels plus a sub, AC-3.

t085.text: But cinemas didn't decide what sound your living-room TV used. Who did?

t086.text: In the US, it went to the FCC, the communications regulator.

t087.text: The digital TV standard on the table named AC-3 for its sound.

t088.text: Remember the company that objected? It was DTS.

t089.text: DTS: ours is better; the standard shouldn't fix an audio format.

t090.text: Dolby: you haven't proved it's better; an extra decoder costs more.

t092.text: December 24, 1996, Christmas Eve: the order passed, with AC-3 for sound.

t093.text: Blunt reasons: DTS hadn't been through the tests Dolby won, nor any independent tests,

t094.text: change could mean delay and cost.

t095.text: So Dolby won and just sat back collecting money?

t096.text: Is it that simple? The same order restated that patent holders

t098.text: Its report admits standards often mean lower rates and less say over who licenses.

t099.text: So I see a standard as a ticket in, and also a leash.

t100.text: But where does this ticket go?

t101.text: The order covered US terrestrial digital TV.

t102.text: Federal rules still say TV stations must transmit to this standard,

t103.text: and tuner TVs must receive it.

t104.text: It didn't cover the world, or your phone,

t105.text: and nowhere says makers must pay Dolby from then on.

t106.text: No rule usually makes phones use it, so why pay?

t107.text: The answer's in a chip: the report says fees usually come in two stages.

t108.text: Chipmakers add Dolby tech, get approval, and sell to device makers.

t109.text: What do chipmakers pay? Just a nominal initial fee.

t110.text: The real money is next: device makers need a license to buy those chips.

t111.text: Remember that opening fee? Usually charged per unit sold.

t114.text: Search the report all you like: it gives no per-unit fee.

t115.text: Remember that 93% at the start? Don't hear it as 93% per unit.

t116.text: It's licensing's share of total revenue, rounded in the report; to be precise, 92.5%.

t117.text: 2024: a billion-plus phones, 200 million TVs, 90 million cars.

t118.text: Volume usually lowers the rate: per unit, cars bring more than TVs, TVs more than phones.

t119.text: Stranger still: some license fees don't carry Dolby's name at all.

t120.text: Patent pools too: several holders jointly license AV compression formats.

t121.text: The name on a device and Dolby getting paid don't always match.

t122.text: Who pays most of the $1.2 billion-plus?

t123.text: TVs and set-top boxes still lead: 34% of fiscal 2025 licensing revenue.

t126.text: The story isn't over: TVs hold the biggest slice, but can they last?

t127.text: In fiscal 2023, TVs were 38% and phones 20%.

t128.text: TV is slipping; the report says mobile rose on acquisitions and contract timing.

t129.text: Remember the ticket? The report itself says broadcast standards keep mattering less.

t130.text: Remember “it must keep persuading” from the start? That's phones.

t131.text: Report: phones usually have no standard; it must keep persuading.

t132.text: And phone makers can drop it easier than TV makers.

t133.text: Decades of fees, still persuading. I find that more interesting than the opening figure.

t134.text: How? You can guess: get content to use it first.

t135.text: In 2021, for example, Apple Music added Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos support.

t136.text: So is that opening line, “no hardware, only patents,” right? One last number to go.

t137.text: Besides licensing, the report lists 7% as products and services, about $100 million. What's that?

t140.text: Next movie, look up: those speakers may be Dolby's.

t141.text: So the “no hardware” half fails, from that London corner to this report: it has always sold its own hardware.

t142.text: The other half holds: the TV and phone you bought aren't Dolby-made.

t143.text: So why do makers pay per unit?

t144.text: Not because of a law, nor one patent.

t145.text: Look back: the letter mailed from Afghanistan, the boxes in a factory corner,

t146.text: a lowly cassette, the Christmas Eve order.

t147.text: From these records, my reading: from cassette decks to phones, it has kept device makers

t148.text: willing to pay per unit for a design and a name.

t151.text: Spotted it on one of your devices today? Tell me which below.

t152.text: This channel sticks to the record. Want to open files with me? Subscribe.
